utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've been asked questions by both of my learned colleagues about the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff and particularly in relation to the apparent membership of a Muslim and I believe possibly a Serb from a party other than the SDS. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other cases from the municipalities you looked at where there were non-Serbs on SDS Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was membership of non-SDS party Serbs common on the Crisis Staffs that you've seen?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where they become the Municipal Crisis Staffs, they do -- usually in April or May, they do sometimes add members who were heads of fairly practical municipal institutions, I think of -- in the case of Bratunac the head of the bus company was added. And I think at that point it was noted that he was not SDS. So I can't say for certain about the party affiliation of these added later people, but the Crisis Staff themselves saw themselves as continuous with the SDS Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, in a series of questions - and this starts from transcript page 4478 - it was put to you by my learned colleague that there were great similarities between the committees for All People's Defence and Self-Protection, the Crisis Staff that was established by the BiH Presidency in September 1991, and the SDS Crisis Staffs. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in particular it was put it to you that their composition and their powers are very similar and that these were sort of precedent for the SDS Crisis Staffs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, regarding these earlier precedents for Crisis Staffs, to your knowledge, was the membership drawn from just one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Particularly in the case of the presidential Crisis Staff, was it drawn from a single political party?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So apart from the possible exception of Bosanski Samac you were aware of, how does this compare to what you've seen of the SDS Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS Crisis Staffs were drawn from one particular ethnic group to defend the interests of that one particular ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'll just move on to another area now. Some questions were put to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Direct Your Honours to transcript page 4510 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: -- that SDS Crisis Staffs and Municipal Crisis Staffs were two totally separate organs and that the SDS had no influence over the Municipal Crisis Staffs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would seek your leave to call up a document. This is 65 ter number 1850. I did send notice of this document, but it's -- although it was originally on our 65 ter list, it was withdrawn, the reason being that this question of two separate bodies, a Crisis Staff and a War Staff, and SDS authority over them was not seen as an issue. It was brought up in cross-examination, so we would seek leave to be able to use this now and perhaps have it MFI'd, and seek your leave in writing to have it added and admitted later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We strongly object, Your Honours. This is not appropriate at all. This document, first, is not on the 65 ter list. Now they are seeking to readmit it at the redirect, during the redirect. Of course we should have had that document before and we would have used it if it was on the 65 ter list, for example, because I don't know what is the document. We might have used it in our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just add, it's been disclosed. It was originally on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I am sorry, that is not the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, if I could just finish what I'm saying perhaps and then I'll be happy to listen to your response. It's footnoted in Ms. Hanson's report. It goes directly to the point which my learned colleague cross-examined her on. It's in her report. She was asked about this very topic, so I can only assume that they must have looked at this document themselves at some point before opening up this line of questioning with Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ruling of this Trial Chamber is that only the documents which are on the 65 ter list which are the part of the -- of the expert report are admitted, therefore, we are put on notice that only the 65 ter documents which are noted in the expert report are to admitted in this case. Therefore, if it's not on the 65 ter list, it doesn't exist for us. It's not -- it is not -- it is not -- it is not a potential exhibit. If we use it, that's a different story. It is disclosed to us. I assume it's disclosed to us. But I think it's completely inappropriate that in the redirect the Prosecution seeks to amend the 65 ter list and admit another document. Then we will be -- we would need to be given time to assess that document and cross-examine the witness on the basis of that document. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I, as it were, take over again, with respect. If the logic of this was followed through -- Your Honours, can I just say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I need to object now. Your Honours, it is Ms. Korner who insisted that there should be only one counsel speaking on behalf of the party during a certain witness's presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but this is outside. This is a matter of principle relating to documents which, of course, is an issue that concerns both sides and the whole case. Your Honours, the logic of what Mr. Zecevic is as follows: The Defence having seen that there is a document in a footnote not on our 65 ter list because we haven't seen the relevance because an issue has not been made clear, and the Defence knowing that that document is not in favour of the argument that they are going to advance to the witness, would be able, in the sure and certain knowledge if Mr. Zecevic's argument is right, that because it wasn't on our 65 ter list because the issue had not been made plain, to cross-examine knowing that if the, as I say, the logic is followed, we would never be able to put in that document in re-examination. And that cannot be right. And what the suggestion here is that the witness should be shown the document, Your Honours should see the document, and then MFI it because it's not on our 65 ter list, although I would hope the relevance is then obvious, we would obviously add it to the list of documents that we would formally apply to put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the -- without gainsaying [Realtime transcript read in error "again saying"] the principle which has been previously enunciated and repeated that this particular report may be exhibited by the Prosecution at this stage subject to the right of the Defence if they wish to further cross-examine on it now that it is an exhibit, an event which was not anticipated by them having regard to where the -- where they were at the time the cross-examination began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The implications of this is that we think that the subject which apparently the document deals with, which, I don't know what the document is, I haven't seen it, but this subject apparently is this dual relation between a Crisis Staff and a War Staff. And if I'm right in assuming that the document actually helps clarify this issue, then I must say that the Chamber is inclined to -- then I must say that the Chamber is inclined to allow the document to be shown because -- simply because this issue is really an important issue that comes out of this witness's testimony. So we need to have the issue clarified and, for that purpose, we would like to see the document. But then in allowing the Prosecution to show it even though it was not on the 65 ter list, then in order to make sure that the Defence is not prejudiced by this, we would allow the Defence to take up that issue subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I lose it, Mr. Zecevic, I just want to indicate that at pages 22 and 23 of page 47 -- 48, lines 22 and 23, the transcript records me as saying "without again saying." What I did say was "gainsaying," one word, g-a-i-n-s-a-y-i-n-g. Without gainsaying the principle. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to put on the record, it is the principle, as I understand, according to the rules and the procedure and the jurisdiction of this court, that the Prosecution must know its case before it starts. That's number 1. Now, if -- I, there is nothing else what I can do since Your Honours have decided as you have decided, but what I would suggest is that my learned friend moves on into another area and then returns to this particular document by first giving me an exact reference in my cross-examination where did I mention anything remotely to this particular document, and giving me the opportunity during the break to review the document. That is what I would suggest as a practical matter. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, but there's a point that perhaps needs to be made, is that we have tried to be deliberately careful and economical in our use of language in admitting this document because we don't want to appear to compromise the principle to which you have referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to go on arguing this, but the point is this: We have always made our position clear. We have said it doesn't matter. It's in our pre-trial brief and it was my opening. It doesn't matter what this body calls itself, whether War Staff or Crisis Staff, it's one and the same thing. The first indication we've had that this is not accepted is through the cross-examination of Mr. Zecevic. Had the pre-trial briefs by the Defence set up chapter and verse as did Your Honour Judge Harhoff invite them to do, this is a real issue, then we would have known. And we cannot be penalised in the way that Mr. Zecevic would like us to be penalised because we have no indication that this an issue. And that is the point that I wish to make. I have no objection to what Mr. Zecevic wants more time, but that is, I think, the issue of principle in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have ruled and let's take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's perhaps first see what the exhibit number. Anna?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, it's not -- 65 ter 1850. I just want to make it clear there has been one point which perhaps has been misunderstood a little. This document is not about the relationship between Crisis Staffs and War Staffs. What this document relates to is the authority or the influence of the SDS party over Municipal Crisis Staffs after the transformation from SDS Crisis Staffs to Municipal Crisis Staff, which was an issue that was raised in cross-examination. So it's a little different from perhaps what you may have got the understanding to be from something I'd said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm speechless, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it during the break and see what comes out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we resume I just wanted to alert counsel that wherever we are, in terms of whichever witness is on the stand, at 1.30 we intend to excuse the witness at that point so that a number of administrative matters with which we have to deal we can deal with in the remaining 15 minutes and take the adjournment at the prescribed time of 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness, I just thought I should take this opportunity to apologise for a slip of the tongue which obviously caused some confusion. I went back over the transcript and directed the witness to the fact that we'd be moving on to an issue concerning the separation between SDS Crisis Staffs and Municipal Crisis Staffs. Then the very next stage when I asked Your Honours for permission to use this document, in the slip of the tongue I referred to the two separate organs as being Crisis Staffs and War Staffs. So I can understand now where the confusion came from and I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn, because if we thought we had heard you correctly, we were prepared to recall the ruling that we had made allowing you to proceed as you had asked. So we are back on track. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And could we call up 65 ter 1850, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, while we are waiting for the document to come up you recall that I had turned to a series of questions that you had been asked about the apparent difference between SDS Crisis Staffs and Municipal Crisis Staffs, and whether the SDS had any influence over Municipal Crisis Staffs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the document in front of you, you'll see that it's from the SDS executive committee. It's dated 31 May 1992, and appears to have been sent to various regional Crisis Staffs. Now in the light of the issues that we've just been discussing, can you review this document. First of all, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it and I refer to it more than once in my report, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in relation to the issues we've just been discussing, can you tell us how, if at all, this relates to authority of SDS, the SDS party over Municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see that it's the SDS instructing the presidents of regional Crisis Staffs to implement the Presidency decision of 31 May on abolishing Crisis Staffs and setting up War Presidencies. Interestingly enough, in the first paragraph, he -- the author confuses War Presidencies and war commissions, even, but he is clearly, by the date, referring to the decision on War Presidencies. I also note in the first sentence that he refers explicitly to Djeric's instructions of 26 April 1992 which would certainly suggest that they were not withdrawn but were regarded, by the SDS at least, as having been setting the framework for the structure and method of work of Crisis Staffs. So it's not purely a municipal matter; it's not purely a state matter; it's the SDS party making sure that the regional Crisis Staffs are helping the implementation of a Presidency decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, and could this document be marked for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We had said it could be exhibited, so it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- tendered, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Next I'd like to call up document 65 ter 637.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, still discussing the same issue, you'll see that this document is from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, dated 19 June 1992. Can you tell us if this has any relevance to the issue of SDS authority over Municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, it indicates the close relationship between the SDS and Municipal Crisis Staffs. This document is from the Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most but it says that the subcommittees of the SDS shall exercise power over the territory of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to a document actually that we looked at earlier today, if we could call up Exhibit P186.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, you were shown this exhibit during cross-examination, and on a couple of occasions yesterday, you tried to explain the context of this document and whether it shows that the 26 April instructions were ever withdrawn but you weren't able to do so. So I'd invite you now, if you could explain the context behind this document and how you assert that it was not withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the versions found in the government archives is in the Latin script with a few typographical errors, and I note that this document withdrawing the instruction says: "An unfinished text had been delivered to you by mistake." The version that we've seen both in government archives and found in the field is a Cyrillic document, so one possible interpretation of this, given the documents found, is that the Latin text with the typographical errors was withdrawn and a different text sent out. Moreover, there is so much evidence that the text as we know it was received and implemented that I cannot regard this as outweighing the variety of evidence I found showing -- including the document we just saw previous to this, indicating that those instructions were considered to be still binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I would refer Your Honours and counsel to footnote 47 of Ms. Hanson's report in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yesterday you were also asked about the formation of war commissions, and referring to paragraph 44 of your report, you were asked by Mr. Pantelic if you agreed that the only logical explanation for the formation of war commissions was that no one had been able to establish any control over Crisis Staffs at the local level. You said you did not agree with this assertion. Could you expand on that, please?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see the issue as Crisis Staffs were running wild and the government was -- or the republican level was trying to get control over them. I see Crisis Staffs as having been formed on the initiative with the instructions of the republican level and receiving instructions, orders from, communicating with the republican level. So I see these steps that I -- the various decisions in May 1992 not as an establishment of control, but more as part of the process of formalising the organs that had previously been SDS organs into state organs of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I don't have objection to this particular question, but in terms of clarity, frankly, I didn't -- I believe I didn't pose this question to witness. Maybe I'm wrong. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It may be my mistake, Mr. Pantelic, and if so, I do apologise. It may have been, yes, Mr. Zecevic. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Finally, it was -- not finally, but it was put to you yesterday that, in 1991, before the Variant A and B instructions were sent out, there were over 900 Crisis Staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you said that these Crisis Staffs are not the same as the Crisis Staffs which are the subject of your report. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you explain what these 900 or so Crisis Staffs were? Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, as I say, the 900. I've been shown a few documents of a Presidency Crisis Staff, HDZ Crisis Staff mentioned, there was mention of a police -- a MUP Crisis Staff. What I have heard from witnesses but not seen in any documents is that "Crisis Staff" was a known term that could be used even [indiscernible] by government organs within an enterprise, within a company or something even to deal with a crisis situation. So my focus is on the municipal organs of the Bosnian Serb state and how they arose from the Crisis Staffs formed within the SDS. So I have really nothing to say about those 900-whatever Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you were asked about Article 12 of the Law on National Defence and basically whether this was the basis for the formation of Crisis Staffs. You responded that your understanding was that it doesn't mention Crisis Staffs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder at this time if we can call this document up; it's 65 ter 8000. Simply it wasn't actually shown at the time and so I would like to see exactly what is said in that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this one on 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To be frank with you, I got this particular article but we didn't find it during cross-examination, so I agree absolutely to show to the witness specifically the last portion of this article. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, what we are looking for is Article 12 of that document. And I just want to make it clear this is the February 1992 law, because I believe there's a later one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, looking at Article 12, is there any mention of Crisis Staffs in there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, I do apologise. Could we have also the rest of the article, the other part of Article 12 in B/C/S, because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you see any mention of Crisis Staffs in that portion of Article 12, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm on to my last few questions. Earlier on this morning you were asked -- well, it was actually put to you that there were two bodies existing at one time in the ARK; a Crisis Staff and a War Staff. Ms. Hanson, in the course of your research, have you seen any document showing that there were these two separate bodies existing at one time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I have no further question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you wish to exercise your right to cross-examine on -- re-cross-examine in respect of the -- those companion documents which were exceptionally exhibited during re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with your permission, if this particular article is applied to this document, if I understand? Article 12 that we just seen? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It was document 1850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, if I could just take you back to your testimony just a little while ago where you said that, in your view, and let me quote you, you did not see the issue as Crisis Staffs were "running wild and that the government was trying to get control over them." So my question would be: If it wasn't a matter of getting control over the Crisis Staffs, then why were they abolished?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb state was in the process of formalising its structures and passing -- we see passing provisions such as for a municipal War Presidency that didn't exist before. And because, as I see -- I see no legislative basis for Crisis Staffs, so they create -- using the previous model of a collective municipal Presidency, they introduce that into the constitution which was not part of the RS constitution until the 2nd of June, 1992. So I see it more of a process of regularising institutions that have been set up by the party, generally secretly, separating from the existing constitutional framework of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, creating their own parallel state and then creating the normative documents to match the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, in your view, it was merely a cosmetic change that was established in order to give them another name but otherwise to allow them as to perform as business as usual with the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not say merely cosmetic. I think there was an element of getting the house in order. Similar as we see the creation of the VRS and the establishment of a command structure there and the police, we see asserting more authority of the ministry at this time, say June/July 1992. I think that Crisis Staffs were set up on the initiative of the party, given a broad mandate to take power. In the take-over of power, they were allowed to use considerable initiative on their own, and once they had established power on the ground, then the Serbian state could be effectively created. And certainly we do see that there's some instances where the state structures felt individual Crisis Staff presidents had gone -- too far gone beyond their mandate and the rule of law should be asserted over them, but I see that as a factor of a product of them having been given their head early on. Given a task, take your initiative, go out and get this done, was what we see in the March Assembly sections. Wait for our instructions, you'll get instructions and then you guys on the ground do it. Once it's been done and the territory is being held and made part of the Bosnian Serb state, then we see the formal structures being regularised. So it's not merely cosmetic but it's not that the Crisis Staffs were spontaneously formed on the ground and had no relation to the higher structures which were the structures that were themselves in the process of changing from party organs to state organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you explain why apparently it was so important for the Bosnian Serb leadership to ensure that the Crisis Staffs were actually abolished and replaced by War Staffs or war commissions? I don't know which term to use now.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "War Staff" I haven't seen enough that I don't use it in my report. Occasionally it's crept in but it could also be refer to more strictly military things, such as the staff of the TO at the time could be called a War Staff. So I'm reluctant to use that term much. I don't think it was all that important because we see some organs calling themselves Crisis Staffs until July. I think that it was not seen as a practical difference. I see the -- Rajlovac saying, Well, we had a War Presidency, then a war commission, and in the War Presidency the tasks were the same. We see the confusion even in that document from Trifko Komad, that within two -- between two paragraphs he confuses commissions and presidencies. I think it was generally understood that they were the same organs and I think that there was an attempt that Crisis Staffs didn't -- the sound of the word "Crisis Staff" didn't coincide or didn't agree with their desire to have a functioning state. If we have established power, we've moved beyond a crisis and now we just need a collective Presidency. But the fact that we see the terms used practically interchangeably and I don't see a very strong dissatisfaction in the top levels that they are still calling them Crisis Staffs -- calling themselves Crisis Staffs, I don't know how much it mattered. I do see I think in July in the government minutes somebody reporting that people on the ground are confused about these terms, but I don't see a government response of, By God, they've got to stop calling them Crisis Staffs. It's more, For ease of understanding, let's all settle on one term. Why the Presidency decision on war commissions of 10 June abolishes both Crisis Staffs and overturns the earlier decision on War Presidencies, I don't understand because I see so few war commissions functioning subsequent to those instructions. And where I do see them functioning, they look exactly like the War Presidencies. And in the Ilidza document, for example, that I mentioned, from January 1993, they use the term apparently interchangeably or inconsistently. So I can't explain that one terribly well, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, let's go back to the more substantive powers that were held by the Crisis Staffs. You told us that the Crisis Staffs began to pop up throughout the municipalities sometime very early in 1992 or perhaps even late 1991, and that certainly by April 1992, they were fully functioning almost everywhere. And you also told us that there were duplicates which was -- which the Defence reminded us of, duplicate in the sense that also the Muslim and the Croat communities set up their own Crisis Staffs. My question to you or the line of questions that I wish to put to you has to do with the functions of the Serbian Crisis Staffs in relation to the armed forces in the area. So I want you to describe to us just how did the Crisis Staffs perform their leadership or control over the various armed forces that were present in each municipality. We are speaking about, first of all, of course, the army, the JNA, and then there might be special units associated with the army, then you have the paramilitary formations, and then, of course, you have the police. How, if you can -- how, if you can describe this to us, how did the Crisis Staffs actually coordinate this? How did they exercise their functions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, this question is the one that has -- that lacks a consistent pattern, the question of the extent of the Crisis Staff control over the various armed forces. One factor was if there was a JNA unit in the municipality, and if so, what its relation to the SDS and the plans of the Bosnian Serbs. We see in the Prijedor example that Colonel Zeljaja is later even boasting about how he was advising the SDS and encouraging them and telling them how best to take over. We see that in the radio broadcast as well. In other places, as Karadzic indicates in his speech from April 1995, in some places the SDS had to hide their plans from the JNA, if the commander, he said, was Uso or Huso, Muslim names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the record and the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. In Karadzic's speech he said that: "Sometimes we had to form our armies in secret where the JNA commander was a Huso or a Uso," meaning a Muslim name. Where there was a standing JNA unit station in the municipality, I see much less control by the Crisis Staff. Although we see, for example, in Zvornik that the commander of the JNA staff is supposed to be a member of the Crisis Staff. Where in some places the SDS set up its own armed units calling them a Serbian TO, again the relation with the TO would depend on who was in charge of the municipal TO. If it was a non-Serb majority municipality, the head of the TO might well be a Muslim or a Croat, in which case the SDS would form its own independent armed units. Another source was the reserve police force, we see A and B instructing the Crisis Staffs to act -- mobilise the reserve police forces from the ranks of Serbs. These, the leaders of these various armed forces were part of the Crisis Staff. They were included within the Crisis Staff. We see the commander of the TO. The head of the police, the commander of the largest army unit or the principal army unit being part of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff brought these various forces together with the common goal of establishing Serbian power in the territory. What I've seen is how they work is they receive reports on the battle-field and general conditions, security conditions from the police commander, the TO commander, the army commander, if there is one, or a representative. By June or July we see rather than the army commander, a representative, which I take to mean -- be an assertion of the VRS as having its own effective command structure now and they will consult with the Crisis Staff but have their own structure. Then decisions are taken collectively on how best to proceed, to defend the territory, to take more territory, to establish Serbian power. And from the discussions, it can vary the extent of the, say, the president's ability of the Crisis Staff to actually order in some places. I know, for example, in Bratunac, the head of the Crisis Staff called himself commander of the TO and said he ordered an attack. In other cases, it would be more collectively, Well, we ought to take this area, or we ought to defend and therefore, okay, the TO will have that tasking. And then the commander of the TO will go back to his unit and implement that decision. But I see it as collective decision-making with a common purpose, and who is issuing specific orders and how they will be implemented differs so much from municipality to municipality that I'd have to look at each one on a basis. In some places we see very clear orders from the Crisis Staff to specific units. In other cases we see simply consultation. In Bosanska Krupa, we can see the change quite clearly because in April we have an order from the Crisis Staff. In May it's a recommendation to the army, and I think that indicates the evolution, the change from direct command to simply a recommendation and a collective effort. The army itself in its review of the history of the VRS notes that some -- that Crisis Staffs form their own infantry brigades and commanded them in the early days. Paramilitaries can be more difficult, simply that they are difficult to define exactly what one person might term a paramilitary, another might say, Well, it's our reserve police force or our Serbian TO, or it's something calling itself a TO group come from another municipality. We see that in Zvornik, for example. So I'd really have to say that has go on a case-by-case basis. I note the -- in the report from Bosanska Krupa, that they say, We had to -- we worked on integrating our TO into the JNA so that we would not be regarded as paramilitaries. It's clear from that report they secretly armed the Serbs, formed their own secret Serbian TO, then sought to integrate it in consultation with the JNA unit in the next municipality so that we would not -- so that they would not appear to be paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the police?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similarly, the police commander was part of the TO. We see many, many examples of orders from the Crisis Staff to the police to carry out various tasks. So I think again it was agreed that the commander of the police usually would brief, report to the Crisis Staff at every session, tasks would be decided collectively and then either the commander would simply take those tasks back or there would be a written order to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Does that include reserve forces as well? Police reserve?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not at the moment recall seeing anything explicit making a distinction between police active -- a Crisis Staff order to reserve forces as opposed to active forces. I see the mobilisation. I'm sorry, I'd have to look at my documents. It doesn't strike me as a distinction that I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. I just wonder, looking at line 22, Ms. Hanson, according to the transcript, said: "Similarly the police commander was part of the TO." I just wondering if that was what was said or what was meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't what I meant. I meant Crisis Staff. I don't know if what I said ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understood as much. Would the Crisis Staff be the appropriate body locally to resubordinate, say, police units to the armed forces or the purpose of a concrete military action or operation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. I could see it happening that because you'd have both the commander of the police and the commander of the armed forces at the Crisis Staff meeting that the issue would be raised. We need more forces for this action, okay, let's subordinate the police. I can't speak to the exact procedure that would be required. From what I see, as they were in the process of setting up their own state and their own municipality, they didn't always follow or didn't even have a letter of a law to follow. We see, for example, in Kotor Varos they take a more distant -- the Crisis Staff takes a more distant approach, saying, We are not going interfere with how you do it, but you, both the armed forces and the police, are responsible for security in the municipality. So it could well happen through the Crisis Staff, but it could be that in a place like Kotor Varos, which seemed to be take keeping a distance, it might not, but they certainly received reports from both the TO and police in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We will move to the regional level in just a little instant, but before we leave the local level, my last question in relation to this is whether the Crisis Staff would also exercise some control over the judiciary that was existing in the municipality. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. It dismissed a lot of members due to officials of the local Prosecutor's Office or courts and named -- almost invariably these were non-Serbs, and named new officers, almost invariably Serbs. I know in Krupa, for example, the Crisis Staff set up a wartime court. We also saw that in Sanski Most. In many places they are setting up specific war time courts. They are dismissing the existing judicial officials and appointing their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of any determination made by one or more Crisis Staffs about the direction of investigations against war crimes committed within the area -- within the local area? Do you understand my questions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Only war crimes committed against Serbs. I have not seen a Crisis Staff ordering an investigation of the treatment of non-Serbs. I do see them receiving Plavsic's instructions about documenting war crimes committed against Serbs and mention of that, although, that's -- I don't recall it being a -- seeing much about that and it may be that it wasn't -- it was not something that I was looking at in particular. But I certainly did not see the Crisis Staffs ordering investigations into crimes against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you saying -- I wish to understand your answer correctly. Are you saying that you have not come across any example of a Crisis Staff ordering investigations and prosecutions against crimes committed by Serbs, war crimes? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move to the regional level because you have given us now your picture of how it worked on the ground, and my question would then be, well, how did all of this relate to the vertical co-ordination with the regional Crisis Staffs above the level of the local Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, the picture, the documentary evidence is so unbalanced that I'm reluctant to draw any conclusions. We can see what was going on in ARK. We can see the close connections to -- between the Municipal Crisis Staffs and the ARK Crisis Staff and the ARK's then connection to the republican level. I think it was a Sanski Most document where we see that for certain problems they say, We'll consult with the ARK and, if necessary, the republican level. But clearly ARK is their first stop. We see ARK, for example, passing on the 31 May Presidency decision and telling the municipalities to carry it out. I don't have anything like that kind of documentary evidence from the other regions, and from the general -- my general understanding of the events of the war, the other regions were simply not -- the other regional organs were simply not as robust, didn't meet as often, didn't have as much to say, and the documentary evidence is so poor that I can't say how they operated. We see that they are there, we certainly see them seeing themselves part of the state, part of the state system, following the line of the SDS, but I don't see enough of those kinds of documents that we see from the ARK for me to say how they operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have made yourself very clear about this in your earlier testimony. Can I just clarify whether this -- these observations also apply to the period after, say, July/August 1992, when the war commissions were taking over?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the late summer of 1992, I believe, the regions were in the process of being abolished, although I'm not quite sure of the exact dates, and again, I don't see war commissions taking over. War commissions, according to the decision of 10 June, were intended to get the municipal organs, particularly the Municipal Assembly running. So if a Municipal Assembly could meet, it would take over. Although in many places, it couldn't meet or didn't meet until August or sometime even in the fall. They preferred to have a small collective body running the municipality instead. Where I do see war commissions operating, they look exactly like a War Presidency. And as we see in Ilidza changed -- or Rajlovac changed their names without changing their structure or function. So although the document indicates -- the 10 June decision would indicate that war commissions should take over everywhere, we don't see commissioners appointed or war commissions appointed everywhere. And as I said, it's -- I can't explain the difference between the stipulations of the 10 June decision that the decision on War Presidencies is superseded because we see them all three bodies existing in June and July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question is if you are aware of any example either on the local level or on the region level of co-operation between the Serbian Crisis Staffs and the Muslim and the Croat Crisis Staffs? Did you ever come across any degree, any examples of --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, co-operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Incidents where they were able -- where they were able to actually meet up and regulate local matters or any attempt to have such co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw no attempt at co-ordination or co-operation like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Hanson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hanson, for -- Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. I think during the -- this part of examination on the question of Honourable Judge Harhoff, certain issues arise so we could have a right for clarification for additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which honestly, Your Honours, having in mind the topics and the, I would say, one huge flow of information that we just seen from Mrs. Hanson in the end of her testimony, I kindly ask you because I need to review and to classify -- to make certain systemisation of parts of her answer, so I kindly ask you for a time that I can proceed with this re-cross on Monday session, because this is a really huge area that she actually now covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to re-cross Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are only thinking that the more efficient way of proceeding may be - especially having regard to the fact that Ms. Hanson is resident within the Tribunal - to coordinate some point at which it would be convenient to -- for you to exercise your right for further cross-examination, rather than fixing it for Monday, because that might throw a spanner in the works of the Prosecution's plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, thank you, Your Honour. I do appreciate your position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe we should ask if Mr. Dobbyn has any questions that he wishes to put to the witness in light of the questions by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I don't have any questions, Your Honour. The only issue is that if Ms. Hanson was to be called later, we would ask that in the meantime she be allowed to communicate with the Prosecution particularly with the Karadzic team for who she is also an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no objections at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That would actually allow us to benefit from Ms. Hanson's testimony if we have sort of an empty spot at some point that we could fill out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pantelic, is there a possibility of your being ready first thing on Monday morning so that if -- even if it involves interrupting the witness then on the stand, then we can get her out of the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour, I'm absolutely ready for Monday morning. To be honest with you, Your Honour, I do apologise, I would be ready even today but I lost my reading glasses so I cannot follow. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, 15 maximum, but 10 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Hanson, you are not released. You are excused but we ask you to return to this courtroom for 9.00 Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm still under oath, therefore not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you are still under oath and the usual warnings apply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: She may now be escorted from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the next witness is Christian Nielsen. However, given your indication that you wanted to deal some procedural matters at 1.30, I would ask that we delay starting him until Monday. A couple of reasons. One is because of in light of an answer Ms. Hanson gave to a question from Judge Harhoff about the Crisis Staff perhaps subordinating police to the army is something that I would like to discuss before he comes on. It's not something that has occurred to me before until I've heard that, and I don't know what else may have arisen with her that it would be beneficial for me to raise them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition -- I'm sorry. In addition, yesterday, I know at the end of the day, Judge Harhoff suggested or asked that the parties get together to give the Chambers a heads-up on the content of his record, and I assume that you meant something by what you had requested from Mr. Dobbyn and Mr. Zecevic at the beginning of Ms. Hanson's testimony. We've had some conversations. I think it would be easier to talk about one or two things we agree on than what we disagree on, if that's fair, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The purpose of the requests made by the Chamber is limited to the expert witnesses because the Chamber believes that when we have to do with expert witnesses, then there is a report, and that it is a huge advantage not only to the Chamber but also to the parties if the parties would indicate their position on the main aspects of the report, what in your view, Mr. Hannis, is the essential conclusions that are made in Mr. Nielsen's report. And where -- and we put the similar question to the Defence, and we would then ask the parties also to indicate where do you disagree on the substance of the report because we think that this will facilitate the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of these witnesses. So that's the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I would defer to Mr. Zecevic on where we disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But you will have plenty of time in the weekend to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would certainly appreciate more time to discuss over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure you have nothing better to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for fear of being impertinent, Your Honours, it will be useful to me, instructive, it will give me good guidance if I know if the Trial Bench has had an opportunity to read the report. Because if you've already read the report, then there's certain things I won't bother to try and bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no, we have read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There are a number of items, the last of which we would go into private session to deal with, but the first one is the -- and this relates to the -- this is relevant to the Prosecution's timing as regards the witnesses who are expected to testify by videolink. The Chamber has determined that although the court resumes on the 11th of January, that that week will be devoted, because counsel would recall that there was an application in respect of the 14th of January to accommodate the Christmas according to the Julian calendar, that the -- that week will not be used for sittings, but the Chamber will use that time in order to dispose of certain outstanding matters, especially adjudicated facts, so that the resumption of hearing would be on the 18th. And the -- my recollection is that the Prosecution had intended that the videolink witnesses would follow in the second week of hearings. So the question for the Prosecution to decide is whether they would retain that second week, which would be the 18th, or whether they would remain with that, and the Registry would require a -- to be -- a firm decision on that before the winter recess begins next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can certainly do that, Your Honour. I think we'll consult and notify witnesses and advise you early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Specifically we would be grateful if we could have by 4.00 p.m. on the 17th, which is yesterday week, the names of -- notice of all the witnesses who the Prosecution intends to call during the week of the 18th and 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The second item is that to -- clarify a ruling -- yes, all the witnesses for the week of the 18th and 25th. The second item is that yesterday the Trial Chamber issued a ruling concerning a missing English translation of a 2003 statement of ST-48. However, the transcript is unclear as to the manner in which the translation is to be provided and it would be insufficient for the Prosecution to put the translation in e-court. So to ensure a complete record, the Prosecution is requested to file the translation by the 14th of December. Is there anything else before we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the parties to give us before the start of the recess the -- not only the planning for the first week's witnesses, but also the estimates of the time needed for the, let's say, the next witnesses for two months or something like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could we move into -- yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Bajagic, who is our expert, would need to be excused [Realtime transcript read in error "executioned"] if we are going into the private session because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for reminding me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I saw that the transcript was saying "executioned." I said "excused."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It is Friday afternoon, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment, Monday morning, 14th, in this courtroom at 9.00. I trust everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
